doc.title: Jimmy Witherspoon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, FL, April 12, 1996

title: Segregation in the 1940s and rock musicians taking from black artists
summary: He describes segregated venues, a Miami beach club, and says prejudice persists; criticizes the Rolling Stones and praises Van Morrison.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Should be an interesting concert tonight. I can’t wait. What was the work like at that time? Were you playing dances? Little clubs?
Dances and big clubs, big ballrooms.
Was the audience at that time segregated.
Sure it was segregated. We had to go in the back of restaurants. I remember a time in Miami, I could go to a club on the beach where the Jewish people couldn’t go.
That’s strange. And this is in the 50s?

No, this is in the ‘40s. This was bad. This was bad. I could go to the beach because I was an entertainer. I could go in the club, but the Jews couldn’t come in. People talk about prejudice, racism and all that, it’s always been and it always will be.
Has the music helped to make it any better?

No. No. What has happened is, you have some wonderful people in music, like Bonnie Raitt, Van Morrison, real, but you’ve got a lot of phonies in the music business, who could help bridge that gap. Like the Rolling Stones, who couldn’t keep a beat if you give them twenty drums. Mick Jagger could learn a lot by putting a black artist on some of his concerts. Do you hear what I’m saying? He’s stolen so much from us. I’m not bitter but I am aware of what they’ve done, and it hurts sometimes. But Van Morrison just called me the other day. He’s called me three times and a couple of times just to say hello. The last time he called, it was four days ago, asking would I play with him in New York for four
